title: Peacock promotion and collateral self-removal
motif: Promotion threat; sweeping friendly-piece removal
evidence: Black’s Peacock takes the Crossbow Soldier at 141, then Water Dragon and Kirin at 143 while promoting to Tengu. White’s intervening Flying General move at 142 removes six friendly pieces along its route.
interpretation: This is not a single hanging-major-piece episode. The concrete patterns are an enemy promotion breakthrough and the cost of clearing a corridor with a sweeping piece. The original depth-4 to depth-3 drop exaggerates how confidently we can locate the mistake.
handling: Check promotion continuations and account for friendly path victims. A quiet escape or preventive move may need main-search coverage; extending only captures need not find it.
test: Review 140–144, especially whether 140 or 142 permits the promotion. Do not require avoidance of the Flying General move until alternatives are shown to improve the position.
pattern_family: Mixed: classical mechanism and variant geometry

title: Correct capture neutralizes a promoted attacker
motif: Defensive capture against multiple threats
evidence: At 67 Black promotes Flying Eagle to Great Eagle on 18,30. From there it has capture routes against White’s Tengu, Peacock and Free King. White’s Kirin captures that Great Eagle at 68, removing the attacker.
interpretation: The apparent collapse is a poor blunder label: the critical observed move is a sensible defensive capture and the subsequent Tengu remains active. The depth-4 and broad-quiescence searches retain the capture.
handling: Keep this as a compensation/defense control. A change should not be rewarded merely for producing a larger score or changing the move.
test: Candidate success is recognizing the defensive capture at 68; do not classify the score drop itself as a tactical miss.

title: A genuine double attack, followed by a later hanging Tengu
motif: Line-based double attack; later ignored direct threat
evidence: At 169 the Flying General reaches 30,18 and can take either Tengu at 35,18 or Bishop General at 16,18. White moves the Tengu at 170 and loses the Bishop General at 171. Later, Fierce Ox moves to 21,10 at 173, and takes the relocated Tengu on 18,13 at 175 after White plays a Woodland Demon promotion at 174.
interpretation: Saving the Tengu at 170 can be a rational response to the double attack; blaming that move for the Bishop General loss would be misleading. The cleaner suspected omission is the separate Tengu threat at 174. These need two subpositions rather than one undifferentiated “lost two majors” label. Follow-up at 174 finds Spear Soldier 22,10–21,10, capturing the attacking Fierce Ox. The rules replay confirms that it removes the Tengu threat; forced depth-4 searches give +5064 for this defense versus +2707 for the played promotion.
handling: Test multiple simultaneous threats, threatened-major quiet escapes, and whether a small attacking piece is overlooked. Distinguish quiescence eligibility from reductions on the escape move.
test: Keep 170 as a double-attack/choice-of-victim case. At 174, test capture of the attacker with Spear Soldier, allowing other sound defenses; replay the opponent’s best continuation before freezing a pass/fail label.
pattern_family: Mixed: double attack and variant geometry

title: Two threats during a sweeping exchange
motif: Competing threats; multi-piece sweep and recapture
evidence: At 32 Black’s Great General can sweep the Tengu file, while Roaring Dog can take the Vice General. The observed Great General sweep occurs at 33, White recaptures it at 34, and Roaring Dog takes the Vice General at 35. Earlier a Fierce Dragon swept another Tengu at 27.
interpretation: This is real tactical complexity, but the Great General recapture materially offsets the first loss. The origin of the damage may precede 32, when the two threats become simultaneous.
handling: Follow capture/recapture sequences through their end and recognize concurrent threats on different squares. Destination-only recapture rules may miss the second branch.
test: Compare defenses at 28–32 and evaluate both the Tengu exchange and the Vice General threat. Do not score “Tengu survives” in isolation.
pattern_family: Mixed: competing threats and sweeping exchanges

title: Great General penetrates the back rank
motif: Sequential corridor sweeps; many small victims
evidence: The Great General removes eleven White pieces on its file at 63, then ten more across the back rank at 67, followed by another sweep at 75. At 62 a separate Dragon Horse route also threatens White’s Free King. White’s actual Lion move to 14,32 at 62 interposes on the Dragon Horse diagonal and removes that Free King capture route.
interpretation: The tactical damage is distributed across many smaller victims. It is not a classical single-piece fork or skewer: this variant’s sweeping movement removes intervening pieces directly. The position is shared with other games and should count as one opening family. The Lion move is therefore a genuine defensive block against one threat, rather than an unrelated quiet move. The sweeping threat is a separate problem.
handling: Test aggregate path captures, continuation after the first sweep, and threat handling when no single landing victim is large. Verify the actual quiescence filters before assigning a cause.
test: Start at 60–62 and follow through at least 67. Judge total exchange damage and prevention of continued access, rather than one large captured piece.

title: Tengu sweep followed by a Vice General chase
motif: Direct sweeping threat; pursuit of an exposed major
evidence: Before White’s move 16, the Fierce Dragon already has a route to sweep the Tengu at 29,35. White moves Vice General elsewhere; the sweep follows at 17. The Vice General then reaches 3,18, where Lion Dog takes it at 21. White gets a Fierce Dragon back at 22.
interpretation: Two concrete losses are present, but there is recapture compensation and an earlier difficult position. The depth-4 search still chooses the played move at 16, so deeper agreement does not validate the defense.
handling: Prioritize direct major threats and assess compensation across multiple moves. A quiet defensive move may be heavily reduced even when capture generation is correct.
test: Analyze 14/16 separately from 18/20. Require a verified alternative that improves the full exchange, not just avoids the first capture.
pattern_family: Mixed: direct threat and sweeping exchange

title: Flying General promotes onto a defended square
motif: Unsafe promotion; major captured by a small piece
evidence: At 396 White moves Flying General from 30,31 to 30,10 and promotes. Black’s Longbow Soldier on 30,9 captures the resulting Flying Crocodile at 397. The move also removes friendly pieces along its path. The original square is already exposed to a Great General sweep.
interpretation: The concrete tactical issue is a bad destination during an escape/promotion choice, rather than a hidden distant recapture. Depth 4 finds the retreat 30,31–30,35 and scores it above the forced played move at the same depth.
handling: Test destination safety after quiet/promotion moves, even when the capturer is small. Check whether promotion ordering or reductions prevent a quiet safe retreat from being searched sufficiently.
test: Use 396, with 394 as lead-in. Compare the retreat against the promotion through Black’s best reply; do not assume the promotion bonus is compensation.

title: Great General offered for a more valuable Tengu
motif: Compensated sacrifice and recapture
evidence: White moves Great General to 15,26 at 350. Black’s Tengu captures it at 351, then White’s Blind Bear recaptures the Tengu at 352. On the seed material scale, the 2,160-point General is exchanged for a 2,495-point Tengu.
interpretation: The prominent “lost Great General” event is not evidence of a blunder: the immediate exchange favors White by about 335 material units. The deeper search retains the played move. The earlier score drop at 344 may concern other play.
handling: Use as a control against overzealous hang pruning. Search must see the small recapturer and the value of the full exchange.
test: At 350, recognize the capture–recapture compensation. Keep 338–344 as a separate unresolved evaluation episode; do not label the trade a loss automatically.

title: One sweep takes Free King and Peacock
motif: Multiple victims on one sweeping route
evidence: Black’s Flying Crocodile reaches 22,24 at 289. Its next route to 22,35 removes White’s Free King, Peacock and six other pieces at 291. White continues a Lion Hawk raid at 290. Recapturing the Crocodile at 294 returns only part of the lost material.
interpretation: The sweep and its large net damage are verified. This is a variant-specific line tactic, not a conventional skewer requiring the front piece to move. The depth-4 reference repeats the played move, so a successful defense remains unproven.
handling: Test aggregate swept victims, major threats away from the last move, and the limits of treating a short recapture as a settled exchange.
test: Start at 288/290; investigate moving a victim, taking the attacker, or interrupting the route under the variant’s rules. Do not assume an ordinary chess-style block stops a sweeping piece.

title: Profitable back-rank raid before recapture
motif: Compensated sweeping sacrifice
evidence: At 78 White’s Great General sweeps across Black’s back rank, taking a Free King, Tengu and eleven other pieces. A Yasha captures the General at 79. The two-move exchange gains White roughly 2,457 seed material units before subsequent play.
interpretation: This directly contradicts the initial “Great General lost” interpretation. Both unrestricted and forced depth-4 searches support the raid. The tactical motif is real, but the observed move is an example of accepting a profitable recapture.
handling: Keep as a positive compensation control. Broad quiescence or hang pruning must not reject a sweeping sacrifice solely because the landing square is defended.
test: At 78, score the total path gain minus the General’s loss. The pre-76 evaluation decline is a separate question.

title: Flying Crocodile left on an attacked file
motif: Hanging major; ignored long-range attack
evidence: The Crocodile moves to 35,17 at 734. Before 738, Right Mountain Eagle on 35,9 has a direct capture route to it. White instead moves Right General; the capture follows at 739. The broad-quiescence search selects a Crocodile retreat along rank 17.
interpretation: The ignored threat and a legal escape are verified. However, controlled depth-4 searches score the retreat +373 versus +454 for the played move. Removing the immediate capture is not sufficient evidence that the retreat improves the whole position. Retain for diagnosis, not as a solved defense.
handling: Test quiet retreats of threatened majors and long-range landing attacks. Separate discovery of the defense from the accuracy of its evaluation.
test: Use 738 and earlier 734/736. Verify the proposed retreat against best replies before accepting it as a ground-truth solution.

title: Bishop General walks into capture while Tengu is threatened
motif: Unsafe landing plus a simultaneous distant threat
evidence: White’s Bishop General moves to 16,19 at 186 and is taken by Side General at 187. At the starting position, Black’s Primordial Dragon already has a capture route from 6,21 to White’s Tengu on 6,35, which it uses at 189. White recaptures that Dragon at 190.
interpretation: This combines an immediate unsafe destination with an independent Tengu threat. Merely rescuing the Bishop General may leave the more valuable loss unchanged. The requested depth-4 unrestricted search did not finish.
handling: Test threatened-major responses across multiple squares, small-piece captures of large movers, and broad coverage of defensive candidates.
test: Inspect 184/186/188 separately. Require a defense evaluated against both Side General and Primordial Dragon threats.
pattern_family: Classical competing threats and unsafe landing

title: Capricorn defense rejected by selective search
motif: Hanging major; missed quiet defense
evidence: Black’s Capricorn reaches 35,22 at 41; White’s Great Master approaches to 33,24 at 42. Black plays a pawn at 43 and loses Capricorn at 44. Prior tracing showed the capture was seen, while a quiet Capricorn retreat was reduced and rejected. Depth 4 and full-depth quiescence find Capricorn alternatives.
interpretation: This is the strongest existing failure case. The mechanism is selective treatment of the defensive line, not absence of the capture from move generation. The new fixed-depth comparison again favors the retreat over the forced pawn move.
handling: Investigate the interaction of root late-move reductions, short non-PV quiescence, and quiet escapes of threatened majors.
test: Keep 43 as the established diagnostic regression. Accept multiple sound Capricorn defenses after reply checking; do not require one arbitrary route.

title: Open file exploited after the Capricorn loss
motif: Sweeping file invasion and follow-up recaptures
evidence: At 54 White’s Flying General sweeps to 22,0, promotes, and removes Black’s Free King plus other pieces. Black’s Rear Standard recaptures at 55, but White’s Hook Mover takes that recapturer at 56 and continues the raid. A separate Hook Mover threat to Great General is already available at 53.
interpretation: The tactic is real, but Black is already badly evaluated following the earlier Capricorn episode. This is correlated with 817/43 and should not count as a separate independent success for an adjustment.
handling: Test capture chains beyond one recapture and simultaneous threats. Moving the recognition point backward may be more useful than extending an already lost position.
test: Analyze 49–53 and the sequence through 58. Label as damage limitation unless a materially better earlier defense is verified.

title: Promotion creates a new sweeping attacker
motif: Promotion breakthrough; delayed corridor attack
evidence: The local promotion exchange at 91–92 is not the main large loss. White’s Free King promotes to Great General at 94, then sweeps file 26 at 100 and the back rank at 102. A Fire Demon also promotes at 96.
interpretation: The verified motif is the change in movement power after promotion and its delayed consequences. The score drop from depth 4 to 3 is substantial, and the depth-4 unrestricted search did not finish here.
handling: Test loud-promotion eligibility, continuations after promotion, and quiet setup moves that create access to the promotion zone.
test: Move the investigative focus to 93/95 as well as 91. Do not require avoiding the locally compensated exchange at 91 without evidence.
pattern_family: Mixed: promotion breakthrough and sweeping geometry

title: Promoted runner threatens a General during royal pressure
motif: Promotion-enabled attack; competing royal/material threats
evidence: White’s Ox Soldier promotes to Running Ox at 146 and captures Black’s Flying General at 150. Before 149, Black’s Crown Prince is attacked, although the King is safe and both royals remain. The Crown Prince is captured at 152 after several King moves.
interpretation: This is not a clean isolated hanging-piece puzzle. The player is balancing royal pressure and material threats; ordinary single-king “in check” intuition does not map directly to the two-royal rules.
handling: Test promotion-created attacks, preservation of the remaining royal, and handling of a threatened major while another royal is attacked.
test: Use 147/149, with 141–146 as lead-in. A useful defense must address survival and material together, not only save the Flying General.
pattern_family: Mixed: promotion attack and two-royal pressure

title: Competing captures followed by unsafe General landings
motif: Mutual threats; unsafe destination; sweeping follow-up
evidence: At 136 White’s Flying General captures Black’s Bishop General on a long sweep. Black replies by taking White’s Free King with Phoenix Master at 137. White then puts Bishop General on 25,12 at 138, where Lion Dog takes it at 139. Tengu and Flying General losses follow at 143/145.
interpretation: This is a chain of distinct tactical decisions, not one four-piece fork. White gets compensation at 136, but the subsequent Bishop General landing is an especially concrete suspect. Later losses cannot all be attributed to the original score-drop decision.
handling: Test independent threats during captures, landing safety, and continuation beyond an apparently favorable initial sweep.
test: Use 136 and 138 as separate subpositions; extend through the Tengu recapture at 144 before assigning an exchange verdict.
pattern_family: Mixed: mutual threats and sweeping exchanges

title: Promotion opens a sweeping route to Peacock
motif: Promotion breakthrough; collateral self-removal; diagonal sweep
evidence: Black’s Free King promotes at 77, then as Great General sweeps file 9 at 81 and a diagonal through White’s Peacock at 83. White’s Flying General move at 82 removes thirteen friendly pieces. At 82 Black also has a back-rank sweep threatening a Tengu.
interpretation: The original decline at 72 precedes the decisive motifs by several turns. There are multiple potential routes, so treating Peacock preservation alone as success would be too narrow.
handling: Test promotion-created sweeps, total victim value along paths, and competing routes. Friendly self-clearing costs also deserve explicit inspection.
test: Use 76/78 for prevention and 80/82 for damage limitation. Verify total material and surviving major threats after any proposed defense.

title: Great General captures successive majors while a runner raids
motif: Sequential sweep; ignored repeated major threats
evidence: Black’s Great General takes Tengu at 583, Bishop General at 585, and Flying General at 587. White spends 582/584/586 promoting and moving a Golden Chariot/Playful Parrot to capture much smaller pieces. The initial Tengu sweep is already available before 582.
interpretation: This is a clear tactical pattern with very poor observed material compensation. Nevertheless White was already negatively evaluated; a complete rescue has not been established.
handling: Test danger prioritization over promotion bonuses and small captures, plus quiet escapes before the next sweeping move.
test: Use 582, 584 and 586 as a linked sequence. Record separate preventable losses rather than assuming one move can save all three pieces.

title: Small recapture distracts from a promotion-created General
motif: Promotion threat and sweeping access
evidence: The Treacherous Fox is captured by Tengu at 461, but it had just taken a Chariot Soldier at 458; that local exchange is nearly balanced on seed values. More significantly, Black’s Free King promotes to Great General at 459, and at 460 it has a diagonal sweeping route through White’s Flying General.
interpretation: The Fox loss is not a convincing explanation of the score drop. The newly created General threat is the stronger tactical lead, even though the opponent chooses other moves in the recorded continuation.
handling: Test promotion threats that exist even when the actual opponent does not immediately exploit them. Observed play alone is not exhaustive evidence.
test: Inspect 458/460 for prevention of the General’s access. Treat the Fox capture as a compensation control, not the main failure target.

title: A Lion Hawk can capture both royals in one move
motif: Immediate double-royal capture threat plus a hanging Tengu
evidence: Lion Hawk captures Gold General and lands on 19,35 at 483. Before 484 both White King and Crown Prince are attacked; a separate Black Tengu route takes White’s Tengu on 22,22. White’s King captures the Lion Hawk at 484; the Tengu capture follows at 485. The exact available Lion Hawk route 19,35–18,35–17,35 captures both White royals in a single compound move. Capturing the Lion Hawk removes this immediate royal-loss threat.
interpretation: This is a verified, distinctive Taikyoku tactic: a two-leg move can remove both remaining royals at once. The King capture is a defense against that threat. The last-royal check helper returns false because two royals remain, so a single-royal-only emergency test is insufficient to describe this position. Whether an earlier or combined defense also saves the Tengu is unresolved.
handling: Prioritize a tactical probe for moves that can capture all remaining royals in one compound move, even when there is more than one royal. Test royal survival before rewarding material preservation.
test: Inspect 480/482 for earlier prevention and 484 for possible combined defenses. Saving Tengu while permitting immediate royal defeat must fail the test.

title: Quiet Shitennou approach creates a long-range capture
motif: Quiet threat preparation; hanging major
evidence: White’s Tengu arrives at 32,15 at 658. Black’s Shitennou moves from 0,17 to 0,16 and then 0,15 at 659/661. After White’s unrelated Gold General move at 662, Shitennou captures Tengu across rank 15 at 663. The threat scan also shows attacks on White’s King and Crown Prince from Shitennou and Black’s Tengu; both royals are under attack.
interpretation: The key preparation consists of quiet moves. Capture-only extensions may see the final capture yet fail to anticipate how the threat is created two turns earlier. This is complicated by simultaneous royal exposure, so a Tengu retreat alone is not an adjudicated solution.
handling: Test quiet checking of major-piece threats in the main search and sufficiently searched escapes once the attack is present.
test: Use 658/660 for anticipation and 662 for response. Verify royal survival as well as Tengu safety; the simple “save the Tengu” condition is inadequate.
pattern_family: Mixed: quiet threat preparation and two-royal pressure

title: Promotion lands beside a small recapturer
motif: Unsafe promotion; second hanging promoted piece
evidence: At 329 Black’s Chariot Soldier moves to 15,29 and promotes to Shitennou. White’s Little Turtle on 16,29 takes it at 330. Black’s previously promoted Running Ox on 26,25 is taken by Horse Soldier at 332.
interpretation: The Shitennou is only 400 on the seed material scale, so a 648-unit “major” filter misses this substantial promotion loss. The original score decline at 325 predates the clearest blunder candidate. At 329, depth 4 instead selects Spear Soldier 21,9–22,9. Controlled searches prefer it by 1103 internal units. This avoids making the unsafe promotion, but the enemy Shitennou also threatens Black’s King, so the broader defense still needs deeper adjudication.
handling: Test promotion landing safety and thresholds based on post-promotion value, including tactically important pieces below the broad major cutoff.
test: Use 329 for the Shitennou and 331 for the Running Ox. A correct classification must account for the value after promotion.

title: Fierce Dragon left attacked, followed by sweeping trades
motif: Hanging major; later compensated sweeps
evidence: Before 25 White’s Great Standard has a direct diagonal capture of Black’s Fierce Dragon on 28,16. Black moves Great Stag; the capture occurs at 26. Separate sweeping exchanges remove Tengus at 30 and 38, with Black recapturing the attackers at 31 and 39.
interpretation: The Fierce Dragon at 25 is the cleaner immediate-threat case. The later Tengu losses must include recapture compensation and should not be lumped into one event. A completed depth-4 search finds a Fierce Dragon sidestep and prefers it over the played move at the same depth.
handling: Test major-piece safety against ordinary long-range attackers and exchange accounting for the later sweeping sequences.
test: Start at 23/25 for the direct threat; treat the exchanges around 29 and 37 as distinct subpositions.
pattern_family: Mixed: hanging piece and sweeping exchanges

title: A latent file sweep exists despite little observed loss
motif: Latent multi-victim sweep; observed play misses the threat
evidence: At 92 Black’s Flying General on 13,2 already has a route to 13,35 that removes White’s Free King, Peacock and other pieces. Black instead continues its Hook Mover activity in the recorded game. The same file sweep is eventually used at 151.
interpretation: This is stronger evidence than the original “no immediate material loss” description. The position contains a concrete large threat even though the opponent delays it. It shares a tactical family with the later slot-806 episodes.
handling: Test threats away from the last capture and aggregate path victims. Benchmark scoring must consider best available replies, not require the opponent to repeat the historical move.
test: Use 90/92 and compare defenses to the immediate file sweep. The actual quiet continuation is not proof that the position is safe.

title: Recapture of one attacker leaves another General en prise
motif: Competing threats; recapture versus saving another piece
evidence: At 108 White’s Great General sweeps Black’s Tengu. Black recaptures that General at 109, then a Go-Between takes Black’s Bishop General at 110. The attacking General also had additional sweeping captures available if left alive.
interpretation: The recapture at 109 has a substantial purpose; choosing to save Bishop General instead could leave the stronger General alive. This resembles an overloaded defensive task, but a forced overload has not been proven.
handling: Test competing captures and the opportunity cost of a recapture. A greedy “save the threatened piece” policy is not sufficient.
test: Inspect 105/107 for earlier prevention. At 109, compare the full consequences of recapturing versus saving Bishop General before labeling either choice wrong.

title: Hook Mover exchange is materially balanced
motif: Equal exchange; attacker removal
evidence: At 48 White’s Capricorn promotes to Hook Mover on 24,11. Black’s Hook Mover captures it at 49, and White’s Lion Hawk recaptures Black’s Hook Mover at 50. Both Hook Movers have the same 6,237 seed value. Before 49 the enemy Hook Mover also attacks Black’s Hook Mover.
interpretation: The visually dramatic loss is an equal exchange, not an uncompensated hanging piece. Later White’s own Flying General even removes a friendly Peacock at 52, illustrating why simple “major disappeared” labels are unsafe.
handling: Keep as an exchange-accounting control. Do not reject the initial capture solely because the moving Hook Mover can be recaptured.
test: Use 49 to ensure the full equal exchange is seen. The original depth-3 decline at 43 remains a separate unresolved issue.

title: Unsafe Fierce Dragon landing amid a latent sweep
motif: Unsafe landing; equal Hook Mover exchange; later multi-victim sweep
evidence: White moves Fierce Dragon to 29,18 at 136; Black’s Horned Hawk on 11,18 captures it at 137. A later Hook Mover loss at 149 is immediately offset by White taking the opposing Hook Mover at 150. Black then uses the long file sweep at 151 to take Free King and Peacock; that sweep was already available at 136.
interpretation: The Fierce Dragon landing is a concrete suspect. The Hook Mover exchange is not an independent loss, and the file sweep is part of the same latent-threat family seen at 92.
handling: Test landing safety and multiple threats, while preserving compensation accounting. Do not count the equal Hook Mover trade as another failed tactic.
test: Use 134/136 for prevention, inspect 148/150 for the choice between a recapture and responding to the file sweep, and group with slot 806/92.
pattern_family: Mixed: unsafe landing and sweeping threats

title: A profitable opening capture does not settle competing threats
motif: Mutual sweeping threats; promotion and counterplay
evidence: Black’s Great General takes a Tengu plus other pieces at 25, then is recaptured at 26; that exchange alone is favorable on seed material. White’s Fierce Dragon already threatens Black’s Tengu and takes it at 28. Black’s Peacock captures a Peacock and promotes at 29, then is captured at 30. A further file sweep at 32 takes Free King and Peacock.
interpretation: This is a complex series of mutual threats. The first General sacrifice should not be penalized in isolation; the unresolved question is whether the wider sequence or an earlier choice allowed disproportionate counterplay.
handling: Test exchange sequences across separate board regions and the opponent’s strongest countercapture, not only recapture on the last destination.
test: Use 23/25/27/29 as separate decisions. Require evaluation of the whole sequence through 35, including both sides’ sacrifices and promotions.

title: Checking intermediate move postpones two major threats
motif: Zwischenzug / intermediate check; competing threats
evidence: Before 332 Black has a Great General sweep to White’s Tengu and a Tengu route to White’s Great General. White’s Phoenix Master capture on 23,5 gives check to Black’s sole remaining Crown Prince on 19,1. The engine’s royal-evasion generator requires Black to respond; the previously listed major-capture routes are unavailable during that response. Black recaptures the Phoenix Master at 333.
interpretation: This is a verified classical checking intermediate move. It buys a tempo against threats elsewhere, at a small material cost. The deeper search retains it. Merely preferring a move that appears to guard a major could be worse if it gives up the forcing tempo.
handling: Preserve check/evasion handling when pruning quiescence. Evaluate forcing intermediate moves before assuming a threatened major must retreat immediately.
test: Use 332 as a positive control for an intermediate check. Follow 333–336 to assess the later defense; do not label the Phoenix Master capture a blunder from its local material loss.

title: Royal exposure is real; the score-drop cause is unresolved
motif: Threatened spare royal; unresolved evaluation decline
evidence: The depth-3 score falls between 428 and 430. No enemy non-royal capture above the 300-unit inspection threshold is found at 430, but a Tengu route 10,28–16,34–17,35 can take White’s Silver General and Crown Prince. White’s King remains safe. The observed continuation initially contains quiet moves and favorable White captures; Black’s Free King promotes at 441.
interpretation: The position does contain royal exposure, but the checks do not establish that it caused the score drop or that the played move makes it worse. Both the played move and the depth-4 alternative leave the Crown Prince capture available. This is not yet a solved tactical test.
handling: Retain for studying spare-royal valuation and search/evaluation stability. Do not infer tactical improvement from a changed move or higher self-score.
test: Exclude from tactical success-rate calculations until a concrete forcing line and a better alternative are demonstrated.

title: Bishop General sacrifice wins a Tengu
motif: Profitable sweep and recapture; separate promotion threat
evidence: White’s Bishop General sweeps to 6,0 at 208 and captures a Tengu plus other pieces, while also removing some friendly pieces. It is recaptured at 209. White still gains roughly 1,452 seed material units over the two moves. The Shitennou loss at 211 is a separate promotion-landing issue.
interpretation: The Bishop General disappearance is a false blunder label. The earlier enemy Free King promotion at 201 and the unsafe Chariot Soldier promotion at 206 deserve separate analysis; they cannot be inferred from the favorable Bishop General trade.
handling: Keep the 208 exchange as a compensation control; separately test unsafe promotion landings and threats from newly promoted sweepers.
test: At 208 accept profitable sacrificial captures when justified. Investigate 200/202 and 206 as separate tactical subpositions rather than rejecting the General sacrifice.
pattern_family: Mixed: profitable sacrifice and sweeping geometry
